title: GAT Practice Exam
description: Mock Exam covering Verbal Antonyms, Analogies, Sentence Completion, Reading Comprehension, and Analytical Reasoning.

questions.questionText:
Directions: Choose the word/phrase that is most opposite in meaning to the word.

PROCEED
questions.explanation: Proceed means move forward, go ahead as planned. Choice E recede means to move backward. Choice A secede means to withdraw or quit. Choice C impede means to slow down.

questions.questionText: ELEVATED
questions.explanation: Elevated means above the ground. Choice A grounded means connected to the earth. Choice D subterranean means beneath the surface.

questions.questionText: ELOQUENT
questions.explanation: Eloquent means articulate. Choice A lucid means clear. Choice B ministerial pertains to a minister. Choice E inarticulate means not eloquent.

questions.questionText: SCRUTINIZE
questions.explanation: Scrutinize means to examine something thoroughly and carefully. Choice A skim means to glance at or read quickly. Choice B devour means to hungrily or greedily consume.

questions.questionText: INFIRM
questions.explanation: Infirm means weak, especially from illness or old age. Choice C robust means very healthy.

questions.questionText: REDUNDANT
questions.explanation: Redundant means superfluous, extra, unneeded. Choice A verbose means using too many words. Choice C prosaic means dull or ordinary. Choice E insufficient means not enough.

questions.questionText: RESILIENT
questions.explanation: Resilient means elastic, easily regaining its original shape. Choice B resinous means composed of resins (particular kinds of particles). Choice C resolute means determined. Choice D inflexible means stiff or rigid. Choice E malleable means moldable or flexible.

questions.questionText: INANE
questions.explanation: Inane means silly or empty. Choice B serious means important or solemn.

questions.questionText: CONFIDANT
questions.explanation: Confidant means a friend, a person you can confide in. Choice C enemy is the opposite of friend.

questions.questionText: OVERWROUGHT
questions.explanation: Overwrought means overcome by nervous agitation or being overexcited. Choice A relaxed means an absence of tension or tightness.

questions.questionText: CHIVALROUS
questions.explanation: Chivalrous means positive or high-minded. Choice A gallant means brave or courageous. Choice B discourteous means not courteous. Choice E vainglorious means marked by excessive pride and vanity.

questions.questionText: MODERATE
questions.explanation: Moderate means to make less intense. Choice D intensify means to make more intense.

questions.questionText: AFFECTION
questions.explanation: Affection means love or liking. Choice B aversion means strong dislike. Choice C disaffection means alienation or resentment. Choice D purity means cleanness, freedom from physical or moral pollution.

questions.questionText: EUPHORIA
questions.explanation: Euphoria means a feeling of well-being or elation. Choice A mandate means an order or command. Choice B intoxicant means a mind-altering substance. Choice D euthanasia means mercy killing. Choice E gloom means sadness or depression.

questions.questionText: DISPARATE
questions.explanation: Disparate means different. Choice A dissimilar means different. Choice B similar means the same or nearly the same. Choice C disconcerted means bewildered or confused. Choice D contrite means repentant.

questions.questionText: INFAMOUS
questions.explanation: Infamous means having a bad reputation. The adjective heinous, choice D, means evil, abominable.

questions.questionText: MANDATORY
questions.explanation: Mandatory means obligatory, ordered. Choice A dispassionate means impartial. Choice D inveterate means deep-seated. Choice E disconsolate means cheerless, unhappy.

questions.questionText: DOWDY
questions.explanation: Dowdy means drab or out of date. Choice A slovenly means untidy. Choice C stylish is the opposite.

questions.questionText: EMPATHY
questions.explanation: Empathy means feeling for others, sympathy. Choice B lack of feeling for others is the opposite.

questions.questionText: TRAVAIL
questions.explanation: The noun travail means toil, hard labor; its opposite here is repose, which means to rest.

questions.questionText: BOMB
questions.explanation: A bomb is American theater terminology for a failure, the opposite of hit.

questions.questionText: DISCRIMINATING
questions.explanation: Discriminating means being able to make fine distinctions. Choice C crass means gross, being unable to make fine distinctions.

questions.questionText: IRONIC
questions.explanation: Ironic means using words to express the opposite of their literal meaning. Choice E literal means exact or verbatim.

questions.questionText: PROFUSE
questions.explanation: Profuse means lavish, lush, or abundant. Choice D sparse means not thickly grown.

questions.questionText: IRASCIBLE
questions.explanation: Irascible means quarrelsome or hot-tempered. Choice B cooperative means agreeable or easygoing.

questions.questionText:
Directions: Select the pair that best expresses a relationship similar to that expressed in the original pair.

TROUPE: PLAYER ::
questions.explanation: A troupe is a group of players or actors. Similarly, a club is a group of members.

questions.questionText: GROWL: HOSTILITY ::
questions.explanation: A growl is a verbal expression of hostility. Similarly, a sigh is a verbal expression of relief.

questions.questionText: CAPTURE: TRAP ::
questions.explanation: A trap is used specifically to capture. Similarly, a mill is used specifically to grind. The relationship type is functional.

questions.questionText: CHILD: HUMAN ::
questions.explanation: A child is a young human being. Similarly, a kitten is a young cat.

questions.questionText: TOOTH: ORTHODONTIST ::
questions.explanation: An orthodontist is a specialist whose field is the care of teeth. Similarly, an arborist is someone who specializes in the care of trees.

questions.questionText: COLD: FRIGID ::
questions.explanation: To be frigid is to be extremely cold. Similarly, to be prudish is to be extremely proper.

questions.questionText: BREAKFAST: DINNER ::
questions.explanation: The nouns describe meals, one of the morning, breakfast, and one of the evening, dinner. The lark is conventionally presented as a dawn singer, and the nightingale is associated with the evening and night.

questions.questionText: WAX: CANDLE ::
questions.explanation: By definition, a candle is an object that is usually made out of wax. Similarly, by definition, a pot is an object that is usually made out of clay.

questions.questionText: STUDENT: DORMITORY ::
questions.explanation: A dormitory is a building that houses or contains students. Similarly, a jail is a building that houses or contains prisoners.

questions.questionText: BANANA: PEEL ::
questions.explanation: A peel is the outside covering of a banana. Similarly, a rind is the outside covering of an orange.

questions.questionText: VIGILANTE: POLICE OFFICER ::
questions.explanation: The first term is an extralegal counterpart of the second. A lynching is an illegal form of execution, as a vigilante differs from a police officer.

questions.questionText: PODIUM: PLATFORM ::
questions.explanation: A podium is a type of small platform. Similarly, a critique is a type of small (short) oration.

questions.questionText: PLAGIARIST: APPROPRIATE ::
questions.explanation: A plagiarist is someone who appropriates written material unlawfully. Similarly, a thief is someone who loots or takes possession of material unlawfully.

questions.questionText: OSSIFY: BONE ::
questions.explanation: To ossify is to cause a substance to harden into bone. Similarly, to fossilize is to cause a substance to harden into stone.

questions.questionText: WATER: CISTERN ::
questions.explanation: A cistern is a container specifically for water. Similarly, a silo is a container specifically for fodder or grain.

questions.questionText: UNTRACTABLE: MALLEABLE ::
questions.explanation: Something that is untractable (not changeable) cannot be malleable (pliable). Similarly, something that is immutable is not changeable.

questions.questionText: SANGUINE: CHEERFUL ::
questions.explanation: By definition, someone who is sanguine is cheerful. Similarly, by definition, someone who is destitute is poor.

questions.questionText: PLOTTER: CABAL ::
questions.explanation: A cabal is a group of political plotters or conspirators. Similarly, a cabinet is a group of political advisors.

questions.questionText: WISE: SAGE ::
questions.explanation: By definition, a sage is someone who is very wise. Similarly, by definition, a voluptuary is someone who is very sensual.

questions.questionText: BOAT: WAKE ::
questions.explanation: A wake is the (aquatic) evidence for the prior passage by a boat. Similarly, a track is the (terrestrial) evidence for the prior passage of a human or animal foot.

questions.questionText: DIRGE: MOURNING ::
questions.explanation: A dirge is a verbal expression of mourning, usually in the form of a song sung at a funeral. Similarly, laughter is the verbal expression of merriment.

questions.questionText: OIL PAINTING: CANVAS ::
questions.explanation: The canvas is the surface on which the oil painting is painted. Similarly, a fresco is painted on wet plaster.

questions.questionText: SPIDER: OCTOPUS ::
questions.explanation: The spider and the octopus are eight-legged animals of land and sea. The locust and the water beetle are six-legged animals of land and sea.

questions.questionText: WAIT: LURK ::
questions.explanation: The second of the two verbs adds sinister overtones to the action of the first-wait : lurk. Move and skulk (to move in a stealthy manner) are similarly related.

questions.questionText: THWART: ABET ::
questions.explanation: The two verbs, thwart and abet, are opposites, like murmur (to make a low, indistinct sound) and caterwaul (to howl shrilly).

questions.questionText:
Directions: Choose the word or set of words for each blank that best fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole.

Churchill was cordial to Beria when they first met, but that was the last show of ________ between them.
questions.explanation: The noun here will follow from the adjective cordial. The best word is amiability, closest of the five choices to cordiality.

questions.questionText: Ignoring the increasing cloudiness and the rumblings in the sky, they opened the ________ picnic basket on the shore of the lake.
questions.explanation: The context suggests an approaching storm, so the missing word must mean something like threatening, a good definition of ominous.

questions.questionText: The primary ________ of the region's cuisine, such as beans, legumes, and pasta, provide high levels of complex carbohydrates and often ________ meat as the primary source of protein in the diet.
questions.explanation: The noun could be components or ingredients, but indemnify makes no sense at all, whereas replace is a reasonable choice.

questions.questionText: The ________ of Darwin's theory of evolution on Victorian religion was to create a bitter ________ of ideas and beliefs.
questions.explanation: A cause-and-effect relationship is set up in this sentence with a negative term required for the second blank suggested by the term bitter.

questions.questionText: America at Sea is a one-volume ________ history that covers the nation's military and commercial activities.
questions.explanation: The title tells us the book is about the American sea history the logical choice is maritime, which means 'of the sea'.

questions.questionText: The eruption of the volcano in January was only ________ of the much larger event in March.
questions.explanation: The context calls for a noun that means predecessor, something that comes first. The best choice is precursor.

questions.questionText: Virginia has adopted detailed new ________ for what students should know in English, history, mathematics, and science.
questions.explanation: A word that means standards is needed here. The best choice is benchmarks, which means 'standards or references from which others can be measured.'

questions.questionText: Truman tried to continue Roosevelt's ________ approach to the Soviet Union, but by 1946, he had adopted a much tougher policy toward the Russians.
questions.explanation: The sentence sets up a contrast situation with the word but. Conciliatory is the only choice that suggests a previously weaker approach.

questions.questionText: As the controversial argument continued, the debaters became more ________ and their remarks became more ________.
questions.explanation: The signal words controversial, more, and more suggest a conflict that increases or intensifies. The only pair that supports these context clues is vehement ... acrimonious.

questions.questionText: The Oxford research team was afraid that sensationalized television reports of its work on paranormal phenomena would undermine its academic ________.
questions.explanation: The correct noun must be something that sensational television coverage would undermine in a university setting. The best choice is credibility, or believability.

questions.questionText: The thought of a nuclear ________ sparked by a misunderstanding poses an awesome ________.
questions.explanation: Notice that you are looking for a word coinciding with thought. Only specter is a type of thought (something that haunts or perturbs the mind), and along with it, holocaust makes good sense.

questions.questionText: Unless the environmentalists can draft a more ________ proposal, the courts will disallow their proposition as too vague.
questions.explanation: The missing adjective is defined as the opposite of too vague by the completed sentence. The context calls for specific, that is, explicit or definite.

questions.questionText: Heavy snows in the passes of the Pyrenees have seriously ________ rescuers trying to reach travelers surprised by the spring blizzards.
questions.explanation: The context indicates the missing verb should mean impeded, kept from moving freely. The use of the adjective seriously eliminates excluded.

questions.questionText: It is difficult to take sides with either party because both of the combatants are so ________ to ________.
questions.explanation: Both 'reluctant ... compromise' and 'hostile ... interference' are plausible, but because many disputing parties would object to interference, choice B is preferable.

questions.questionText: The success of the English-Spanish simulcast must be ________ to Margo Quiroz, who interprets 40 different news items in each nightly newscast.
questions.explanation: The context requires a transitive verb used with the preposition to meaning assign or ascribe. The best fit is attributed.

questions.questionText: Time and time again, the power of the mob in Chicago appears to have been annihilated, but it has always ________ itself.
questions.explanation: The but indicates the power has not been annihilated, so the verb that is missing must indicate a rebirth and be used with itself (regenerated).

questions.questionText: One cannot ________ to be impressed by the structural and ________ differences between the United States as a federal union in 1789 and the United States as a federal union today.
questions.explanation: The best choice is fail ... operational. The signal here is cannot ... to be impressed, which should be a negative word, and operational complements structural.

questions.questionText: Comparing him to P.T. Barnum, Mencken called William Jennings Bryan a ________, a mountebank, a fake without shame or dignity.
questions.explanation: The best choice will mean something like fake and mountebank. A charlatan is a mountebank.

questions.questionText: He ________ into the room as if he had just been ________ from a deep sleep.
questions.explanation: Both roused and awakened are good choices for the second blank, but the verb shamble (to shuffle) describes the gait of someone just awakened better than swaggered.

questions.questionText: Unless the prevailing ________ attitude toward genetically altered food is changed, the biotech industry will have little ________ to pursue research and development.
questions.explanation: The missing noun must mean something like motive or reason, and to make sense, the adjective in the right choice should be derogatory, making 'negative ... incentive' correct.

questions.questionText: Alarmist newspaper stories present the pit bull terrier as ________ killer, but owners insist that the dog is friendly and ________.
questions.explanation: The first adjective will be negative (a ferocious killer), while the second must go well with friendly and describe a dog. The best choice is docile.

questions.questionText: Rather than ________ the commuter delays, the new toll road has ________ the problems, and the traffic jams are worse than ever.
questions.explanation: Because the traffic jams are worse, the second word must mean something like increased. The first word must mean something like reduce, leaving only alleviate ... aggravated.

questions.questionText: That so shameless, sentimental, and dishonest a film attracts a large and enthusiastic audience is ________ of how low the popular taste has ________.
questions.explanation: The word low tells us the second word must be fallen, descended, or plummeted. A barometer is synonymous with gauge or indication.

questions.questionText: The show is worth seeing for the ________ of Judy Convoy's vivacious performance, which ________ the stage whenever she appears.
questions.explanation: The phrase vivacious performance suggests that both the missing words should suggest liveliness. Only choice A has a verb that also suggests vitality.

questions.questionText: The company's ________ to produce new, daring, and socially relevant plays has made it the most ________, though not the most popular, theater group in the city.
questions.explanation: Only commitment ... provocative makes sense, with provocative fitting well with the phrase 'though not the most popular'.

questions.passage:
The railroads played a key role in the settlement of the West. They provided relatively easy access to the region for the first time, and they also actively recruited farmers to settle there. The railroads are criticized for their part in settling the West too rapidly, with its resultant economic unrest. Of course there were abuses connected with building and operating the railroads, but it must be pointed out that they performed a useful service in extending the frontier and helping to achieve national unity.

The real tragedy of the rapid settlement of the Great Plains was the shameful way in which the American Indians were treated. Threatened with the destruction of their whole mode of life, the Indians fought back savagely. Justice was almost entirely on the Indians' side. The land was clearly theirs; frequently their title was legally certified by a treaty negotiated with the federal government. The Indians, however, lacked the military force and the political power to protect this right. Not only did white men encroach upon the Indians' hunting grounds, but they rapidly destroyed the Indians' principal means of subsistence-the buffalo. By 1869, the railroads had cut the herd in half, and by the middle of the 1880s, both the southern and northern herd were eliminated. The white man frequently killed the buffalo merely for sport, leaving the valuable carcass to rot in the sun.

The plains Indians were considered different from the Indians encountered by the English colonists on the Atlantic coast. Mounted on horses, typical plains Indians were fierce warriors who could shoot arrows with surprising accuracy while galloping at top speed. Although they quickly adapted themselves to the use of the rifle, the Indians were not equal to the firepower of the United States Army and thus were doomed to defeat.

Theoretically, at least, the government tried to be fair to the Indians, but all too often the Indian agents were either too indifferent or corrupt to carry out the government's promises conscientiously. The army frequently ignored the Indian Bureau and failed to coordinate its policies with the civilians who were nominally in charge of Indian affairs. The settlers hated and feared the Indians and wanted them exterminated. This barbaric attitude is certainly not excusable, but it is understandable in the context of the time.
questions.questionText: The author's attitude toward the treatment of American Indians by whites is one of
questions.explanation: Although the author does not express violent anger, the characterization of the treatment of the Indians as a tragedy and the pronouncement that the whites' behavior was barbaric certainly express strong disapproval.

questions.questionText: The author implies which of the following about the forces at work during the settlement of the Great Plains?
options: The federal government represented the moral use of law.
Justice was overcome by military firepower.
Attempts by the government to be fair were rejected by the Indians.
The settlers' hatred and fear was offset by the Indians' attempts at kindness.
The Indians and the white settlers shared a sporting interest in the hunting of buffalo.
questions.explanation: Although justice was on the Indians' side (second paragraph), the Indians were not equal to the firepower of the United States Army. Each of the other choices contradicts information in the passage.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is concrete evidence that the white settlers did not need the buffalo for their own subsistence, as did the Indians?
options: More than half of the great buffalo herd had disappeared by 1869.
Nearly 15 million buffalo were killed within 20 years.
Buffalo carcasses were left rotting in the sun by whites.
The railroad brought necessary food and supplies to the white settlers from the East.
The white settlers had their own hunting grounds separate from the Indians'.
questions.explanation: This is evidence that the whites killed buffalo for sport rather than for subsistence.

questions.questionText: What is the point of the comparison between the plains Indians and the Indians encountered on the Atlantic coast?
options: The Atlantic coast Indians were not as abused by white settlers.
Because they were considerably better warriors than the Atlantic coast Indians, the plains Indians were a match for the United States military.
If Indians such as those on the Atlantic coast had populated the plains, there would have been no bloodshed of the white settlement.
The Indians encountered by English colonists posed no violent threat to the colonists.
The Atlantic coast Indians were unfamiliar with horses.
questions.explanation: The point of comparison is that the Atlantic coast Indians were not fierce warriors like the plains Indians. Thus they did not pose any kind of violent threat.

questions.questionText: Which of the following characteristics of the passage suggests that the abuse of the Indians is a more significant topic for the author than the beneficial role of the railroads?
options: the statement that the railroads 'are criticized for their part in settling the West too rapidly'
the amount of discussion devoted to the abuse of the Indians.
the reliance on statistical details in both the first and second paragraphs.
the mention of the plains Indians' ability to fight.
the perception that the achievement of national unity was one of the services that the railroad performed.
questions.explanation: Three of the four paragraphs of the passage are devoted to discussing the abuse of the plains Indians. The 'weight' the author gives to this topic suggests its significance.

questions.questionText: The author of the passage would most likely disagree that
options: the United States government's policies toward the American Indians were shameful.
the land that the Indians fought to retain belonged to them.
numerous abuses were among the results of the railroads' rapid spread westward.
some American Indian tribes used sophisticated weapons brought by settlers.
the United States army could not be considered a friend of the American Indian.
questions.explanation: The author states that the government itself tried to be fair but that the agents' indifference or corruption failed the American Indians.

The railroads are criticized for their part in settling the West too rapidly, with its resultant economic unrest. Of course there were abuses connected with building and operating the railroads, but it must be pointed out that they performed a useful service in extending the frontier and helping to achieve national unity.

The real tragedy of the rapid settlement of the Great Plains was the shameful way in which the American Indians were treated. Threatened with the destruction of their whole mode of life, the Indians fought back savagely. Justice was almost entirely on the Indians' side. The land was clearly theirs; frequently their title was legally certified by a treaty negotiated with the federal government. The Indians, however, lacked the military force and the political power to protect this right. Not only did white men encroach upon the Indians' hunting grounds, but they rapidly destroyed the Indians' principal means of subsistence-the buffalo. By 1869, the railroads had cut the herd in half, and by the middle of the 1880s, both the southern and northern herd were eliminated. The white man frequently killed the buffalo merely for sport, leaving the valuable carcass to rot in the sun.

The plains Indians were considered different from the Indians encountered by the English colonists on the Atlantic coast. Mounted on horses, typical plains Indians were fierce warriors who could shoot arrows with surprising accuracy while galloping at top speed. Although they quickly adapted themselves to the use of the rifle, the Indians were not equal to the firepower of the United States Army and thus were doomed to defeat.

Theoretically, at least, the government tried to be fair to the Indians, but all too often the Indian agents were either too indifferent or corrupt to carry out the government's promises conscientiously. The army frequently ignored the Indian Bureau and failed to coordinate its policies with the civilians who were nominally in charge of Indian affairs. The settlers hated and feared the Indians and wanted them exterminated. This barbaric attitude is certainly not excusable, but it is understandable in the context of the time.
questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that the purpose of the Indian Bureau was to
options: try Indians who violated the laws of the new territory.
establish reservations where the peaceful American Indians would live.
assist with Indian affairs and policies of the government regarding the American Indian.
bring to justice white settlers who treated the Indians in a savage or unlawful manner.
assist the Indians in learning a new method of procuring food to rely less on buffalo meat.
questions.explanation: According to the final paragraph of the passage, the Indian agents were either too indifferent or corrupt to carry out the government's promises conscientiously.

questions.passage: In clean air, the human lung capacity will increase for the first 20 years of life, then begin to decrease slowly. But in areas with heavy air pollution, lung capacity growth is slowed. Breathing high levels of ozone or of sulfur and nitrogen oxides lessens the growth of lung capacity and increases the speed of its deterioration in later life. Adults who spend all their lives in bad air may have as much as 75% less lung capacity than those who have lived in unpolluted air. The loss of both the large and small airways of the lungs, narrowed by the unclean air, results in the inefficient supply of oxygen to the organs of the body. The lungs do not recover over time, and the ozone of Los Angeles and the sulfates and hydrocarbons of industrialized eastern cities are equally pernicious. The victims of air pollution are unlikely to be aware of what they have lost; they are so accustomed to shorter breath and coughs that they vigorously deny that they have been affected at all.
questions.questionText: Which of the following most accurately describes this passage?
options: a description of a specific experiment.
a summary report of scientific findings.
a confirmation of an earlier theory.
a refutation of an earlier theory.
questions.explanation: The passage summarizes findings about the effects of several kinds of unclean air on the human lungs throughout a lifetime. No mention is made of the earlier theories.

questions.passage:
Let us consider a hypothetical pair of communicants, utterer and interpreter, from the operation point of view. We shall assume that our utterer has six hats: red, blue, yellow, black, gray, and white. If the rods and cones (the tiny end organs packed together on what corresponds to the sensitive films in the stereoscopic or double-lens camera) of the retinae of his eyes are not defective, he will be able to see that the six hats differ even though they are of the same shape and material. If we reduce the light so that he can barely see, the white and the yellow will seem to be the same. But as the light grows stronger he will be able to see that the red, blue, and yellow affect him differently from black, gray, and white.

He now has sufficient experience (remember, this is all grossly oversimplified) to conceive of color and shade. But he can also distinguish the red hat from the blue and yellow hats, the yellow from the blue and red, and so forth. He is thus ready for the concepts red, blue, and yellow if, for example, we provide him with a red feather, a blue feather, and a yellow feather. Indeed, he may have the human impulse to decorate the hat with the corresponding feather. And if the feathers seem to have more in common with the white hat than the color hats have in common with the white hat, he can see that his concept of shade will determine the difference between the two reds, the two blues, or the two yellows, and he will have need of the concepts of light and dark.

As we increase the number of shades he will require relation concepts like those expressed in the suffixes -er and -est. By repeating the conventional symbols 'hat' and 'red' with the red hat, he conditions the sound of the words to the sight of the hat. If he sees that the relation of each feather to its hat is similar to the other two, he has need of a relation concept like the one expressed by the preposition 'in,' and he is thus prepared to say to himself 'light red feather in dark red hat.'

Now in the dark he is not able to tell one hat or one feather from another but in the middle of a moonless night he is able to think 'red feather in red hat' simply by uttering the appropriate symbols to himself. And with his human impulse to try new combinations, he can even think, 'yellow feather in blue hat' without ever having seen them thus combined.
questions.questionText:
By discussing the different effects of reduced and increased light, the author is
I. pointing to a limitation in the dependence on perception by sight.
II. preparing to discuss the concepts of light and dark.
III. laying the ground for the distinction between what can be seen and what can be thought.
questions.explanation: The discussion shows how perception by sight is determined by the availability of light and looks ahead to the conclusion that the imagination can work in darkness.

questions.passage:
Many people seem to think that science fiction is typified by the covers of some of the old pulp magazines; the Bug-Eyed Monster, embodying every trait and feature that most people find repulsive, is about to grab, and presumably ravish, a sweet, blonde, curvaceous, scantily-clad Earth girl. This is unfortunate because it demeans and degrades a worthwhile and even important literary endeavor. In contrast to this unwarranted stereotype, science fiction rarely emphasizes sex, and when it does, it is more discreet than other contemporary fiction. Instead, the basic interest of science fiction lies in the relation between man and his technology and between man and the universe. Science fiction is a literature of change and a literature of the future, and while it would be foolish to claim that science fiction is a major literary genre at this time, the aspects of human life that it considers make it well worth reading and studying-for no other literary form does quite the same things.

What is science fiction? It is a literary subgenre that postulates a change (for human beings) from conditions as we know them and follows the implications of these changes to a conclusion. That science fiction is a literary subgenre is a point that is often overlooked. Specifically, science fiction is either a short story or a novel. There are only a few poems and plays that could be called science fiction, with Karel Capek's RUR being the only play that is well known.

To say that science fiction is a subgenre of prose fiction is to say that it has all the basic characteristics and serves the same basic functions in much the same way as prose fiction in general. Everything that can be said about prose fiction, in general, applies to science fiction. Every piece of science fiction, whether short story or novel, must have a narrator, a story, a plot, a setting, characters, language, and theme. And like any prose, the themes of science fiction are concerned with interpreting man's nature and experience in relation to the world around him. Themes in science fiction are constructed and presented in exactly the same ways that themes are dealt with in any other kind of fiction. They are the result of a particular combination of narrator, story, plot, character, setting, and language. In short, the reasons for reading and enjoying science fiction, and the ways of studying and analyzing it, are basically the same as they would be for any other story or novel.
questions.questionText: Although few examples of science fiction written before 1900 exist, you can infer that it has been most popular in the twentieth century because
options: with the growth of literacy, the size of the reading public has increased.
competition from television and film has created a demand for more exciting fiction.
science fiction is easier to understand than other kinds of fiction.
the increased importance of technology in our lives has given science fiction an increased relevance.
other media have captured the large audience that read novels in the nineteenth century.
questions.explanation: Because science fiction is concerned with the relation between man and his technology, it follows that as technology becomes more important, the fiction of technology would become more popular.

To say that science fiction is a subgenre of prose fiction is to say that it has all the basic characteristics and serves the same basic functions in much the same way as prose fiction in general. Everything that can be said about prose fiction, in general, applies to science fiction. Every piece of science fiction, whether short story or novel, must have a narrator, a story, a plot, a setting, characters, language, and theme. And like any prose, the themes of science fiction are concerned with interpreting man's nature and experience in relation to the world around him. Themes in science fiction are constructed and presented in exactly the same ways that themes are dealt with in any other kind of fiction. They are the result of a particular combination of narrator, story, plot, character, setting, and language. In short, the reasons for reading and enjoying science fiction, and the ways of studying and analyzing it, are basically the same as they would be for any other story or novel.
questions.questionText: The author believes that, when compared to other literary genres, science fiction is
options: deficient in its use of narrators.
unable to be adapted to drama.
a minor but worthwhile kind of fiction.
more concerned with plot than with theme.
in need of a unique literary approach if it is to be properly understood.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says science fiction is not a major literary genre but well worth reading and studying.

questions.passage:
Many people seem to think that science fiction is typified by the covers of some of the old pulp magazines; the Bug-Eyed Monster, embodying every trait and feature that most people find repulsive, is about to grab, and presumably ravish, a sweet, blonde, curvaceous, scantily-clad Earth girl. This is unfortunate because it demeans and degrades a worthwhile and even important literary endeavor. In contrast to this unwarranted stereotype, science fiction rarely emphasizes sex, and when it does, it is more discreet than other contemporary fiction. Instead, the basic interest of science fiction lies in the relation between man and his technology and between man and the universe. Science fiction is a literature of change and a literature of the future, and while it would be foolish to claim that science fiction is a major literary genre at this time, the aspects of human life that it considers make it well worth reading and studying-for no other literary form does quite the same things.

questions.explanation: The theme is the controlling idea or meaning of a work of literature.

questions.questionText: One implication of the final sentence in the passage is that
options: the reader should turn next to commentaries on general fiction.
there is no reason for any reader not to like science fiction.
the reader should compare other novels and stories to science fiction.
there are reasons for enjoying science fiction.
those who can appreciate other prose fiction can appreciate science fiction.
questions.explanation: The final sentence presents a general comparison between any other story or novel and science fiction, emphasizing their similarities and thus suggesting that the subgenre of science fiction should be read as one reads fiction in general.

questions.questionText: An appropriate title for this passage would be
options: On the Inaccuracies of Pulp Magazines.
Toward a Definition of Science Fiction.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph leads up to the central question-What is science fiction? All of the passage is an attempt to answer that question.

questions.premise:
Three men (Tahir, Pervaiz and Javed) and three women (Elena, Ayesha and Kiran) are spending a few months at Abbottabad. They are to stay in a row of nine cottages, each one living in his or her own cottage. There are no others staying in the same row of houses.
1. Ayesha, Tahir and Javed do not want to stay in any cottage, which is at the end of the row.
2. Elena and Ayesha are unwilling to stay besides any occupied cottage.
3. Kiran is next to Pervaiz and Javed.
4. Between Ayesha and Javed's cottage there is just one vacant house.
5. None of the girls occupies adjacent cottages.
6. The house occupied by Tahir is next to an end cottage.
questions.questionText: Which of the above statements can be said to have been derived from two other statements?
questions.explanation: Statement 5 is the one that is derived from Statement 2 and Statement 3 because in these two statements girls are not surrounded by boys.
